name: ruined flagstone court sinking into a packed-earth yard, ground autotile seen top-down 3/4 (flat ground): pale irregular limestone slabs with mossy joints in the middle; toward the edges the paving breaks up raggedly — slabs cracked, chipped and missing, loose slab fragments and chips lying on the tamped reddish-brown earth, a faint shadow under the slab lips; no kerb; the packed-earth yard is bordered by grass
label: beodeul_yard/flag_dirt

surfaces.part: flagstone paving patch on packed-earth yard, drawn flat top-down

answer.evidence: This is a flat ground autotile seen from above: an irregular paving patch of limestone slabs on reddish-brown earth, bordered by grass. The column scans show alternating slab, joint and earth runs, with no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. Slab lips only have faint shadows that read as flat ground texture. No standing volume is drawn, so there is no front face of 3 or more rows, which matches a terrain tile rather than an object.

styleAnswer.evidence: Measured facts are fine: 10 visible tones per tile (above the paving reference at 7 and grass at 3), only 2% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted. By eye, the slabs are small, uniform cream polygons with thin dark crack lines. Each slab has only about 3-4 lightness steps (cream, light, tan shadow, brown crack) and no per-stone highlight or shading like Beodeul's 5-6 steps. The earth is mid-brown with sparse speckles and a few yellow flecks, so it reads fairly flat and sticker-like. The grass border is a repeated tuft pattern, but it is similar to the reference. The paving is a noisy mosaic of tiny cracked pieces rather than irregular limestone slabs with mossy joints, and I can see little moss. Slab edges have some shadow, but the broken edge is more of a clean-cut silhouette than ragged chipped slabs with fragments scattered over the earth. Overall it is a competent piece but a bit shallower than the references in shading depth and per-material ramps, so I fail it when in doubt.

surfaces.part: flagstone paving patch (irregular limestone slabs with mossy joints)

answer.evidence: The image is a flat ground autotile block seen from above: a full 288-wide field of grass around a reddish-brown earth yard, with an irregular patch of pale cracked slabs in the middle. The column scans show only ground texture runs (earth, slab, grass) with no front-edge line, eave shadow or vertical south face. This is a terrain tile, not a standing object, so there is no top-plus-front structure to measure. Per the definition, with no front face it is a flat top-down slab. This matches the flat-ground intent of the kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: On the primary facts the candidate is at or above the references: 10 visible tones per tile against 7 for paving and 3 for grass, 2% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edges. The tints are therefore real, and the cracks and the earth rim read as dark brown and tan, not black. By eye the slab field is built from many small, individually shaded cream fragments with darker tan cracks, about 4 steps. The packed earth has grain, pebbles, chips and speckle dots, so it is not a flat fill. The grass border matches the reference grass in tone and tuft style. The edges break up raggedly, with chips and fragments lying on the earth, as the brief asks. Weaknesses: the earth ramp is only about 3-4 steps, and the moss in the joints is barely visible. The slabs are a bit uniform and small, so the court reads more like cobble crazing than large limestone slabs. A careful artist would still accept it next to the reference, because it is not sticker-like and has no large flat areas.

surfaces.part: flagstone paving and packed-earth yard ground plane, seen flat from above

answer.evidence: The image is a flat ground autotile: a full-width 288px rectangle of grass, a packed-earth yard and pale cracked flagstones, all drawn as a horizontal plane. There is no standing volume, no front-edge line with eave shadow, no ellipse, no roof and no vertical south face (0 rows). The faint shadows under the slab lips are only ground-level relief. styleAnswer.evidence: Measured facts are fine: 10 visible tones per tile (above paving 7 and grass 3), near-flat coverage 2%, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted brown and not a black sticker line. By eye the candidate still falls short of the Beodeul standard. The slabs are a dense mesh of small, similar-sized cream polygons with thin crack lines and only about 3-4 limestone steps, so they read as a cobble or crazy-paving pattern and not as large irregular slabs with per-slab shading. The mossy joints are barely visible, with only a few green pixels. The earth is a fairly flat brown with sparse specks, and the grass border is a uniform mid green with small tufts, shallower than the reference grass clumps. The ragged break-up toward the edges is there, with chips and fragments, but the shadow under the slab lips is weak. Overall it is competent but shallower in shading steps and ramp variety than the references, and the slab and earth areas lack the layered grain of Beodeul. When in doubt, fail.
